title: Hardness of 6-coloring 3-colorable graphs
formal: Is there a deterministic polynomial-time many-one reduction R from Boolean 3-SAT to finite simple undirected graphs such that, for every 3-CNF formula F, satisfiability of F implies \(\chi (R(F))\le 3\) and unsatisfiability of F implies \(\chi (R(F))>6\)?
definitions: A 3-CNF formula is a conjunction of clauses containing at most three literals, each literal being a Boolean variable or its negation; the formula and variable indices have a standard explicit finite binary encoding. R is a uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine that outputs a graph as a labelled vertex set \(\{1,\ldots ,n\}\) and a list of unordered pairs of distinct vertices, with no repeated edges. Its total running time and output length are bounded by one polynomial in the formula’s encoding length. A proper k-colouring assigns one of \(\{1,\ldots ,k\}\) to each vertex so that endpoints of every edge receive different colours. \(\chi (G)\) is the least such k, with \(\chi\) of the empty graph taken to be zero. The promise decision problem, also denoted \(PCSP(K_{3},K_{6})\), has yes-instances \(\chi \le 3\) and no-instances \(\chi >6\); graphs with \(\chi =4,5,6\) are outside the promise. \(K_{k}\) is the loopless complete graph on k vertices. No colouring or satisfiability witness is supplied as input. The reduction must satisfy the two implications unconditionally, without a Unique Games or Label Cover hardness hypothesis. Because 3-SAT is NP-complete, this reduction is precisely the usual deterministic many-one NP-hardness target for the promise problem.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation, with all definitions, promises, resource bounds and quantifiers as stated. A conditional result establishes only the explicitly conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-verified proof of the full target.
why: Resolve the next concrete constant-palette hardness case in approximate colouring and finite-template promise CSP.

importance.reason: A widely recognized frontier example for promise constraint satisfaction, explicitly posed beyond the known five-colour hardness. Kept separately from the all-constant algorithm question because it asks for an individually significant fixed-template reduction.

progress.text: Barto–Bulín–Krokhin–Opršal establish the 3-versus-5 hardness result within their algebraic PCSP framework.
The introductory discussion of Beyond PCSP(1-in-3,NAE) explicitly asks about six-colouring promised three-colourable graphs.
Bansal–Huang–Lee improve a growing-colour algorithm; a bound depending on n does not supply a fixed six-colour algorithm.

context_blocks.text: The input promise says that three colours suffice, but it does not reveal the three colour classes. Allowing a larger palette relaxes the output condition. The associated gap decision task distinguishes such promised yes-instances from graphs that cannot be coloured even with six colours. This isolates a small finite-template promise CSP with a particularly clear combinatorial meaning.

Barto, Bulín, Krokhin and Opršal establish hardness for colouring k-colourable graphs with \(2k- 1\) colours, including the 3-versus-5 case. The 3-versus-6 question remains explicitly posed in subsequent work. Increasing the permitted palette weakens the output requirement, so hardness at five colours does not imply hardness at six.

TCS-6637 asks whether some fixed constant C admits a polynomial-time colouring algorithm for every 3-colourable graph. A negative result for six colours alone does not exclude algorithms using seven, one hundred or another fixed palette. Conversely, an algorithm with a growing number of colours does not settle even the six-colour search problem. The new card is a precise frontier case, rather than a duplicate of the quantifier over arbitrary constants.

The decision and search tasks should also be kept distinct. A polynomial-time six-colouring algorithm on 3-colourable inputs would decide the gap by checking its output: on a graph requiring more than six colours, no valid output exists. This implication explains the algorithmic relevance of the decision hardness target without redefining NP-hardness as a blanket statement about every search reduction.

The six-colour case has value beyond its small numerical parameters. It tests how far promise relaxation can preserve intractability after the classical CSP dichotomy, and it provides a fixed finite object on which algebraic and combinatorial limitations can be stated. Its specialist home remains Constraint satisfaction under the catalogue’s graph-category expansion.
